html:
The Mamluk Sultanate ruled Egypt, Syria and the Hejaz from Cairo between 1250 and 1517. Its rulers were mamluks: soldiers bought as boys, mostly Turks and later Circassians, trained in barracks and then freed. It is the later half of the chart's Ayyubid and Mamluk Egypt bar.

The mamluks seized power from their Ayyubid masters in 1250. Ten years later, at Ain Jalut, they beat a Mongol army, the first serious check on the Mongol conquests in the west. Under Baybars and Qalawun they took the last Crusader states, ending with Acre in 1291. Baybars also set up a line of Abbasid caliphs in Cairo, after the Mongols had killed the last one in Baghdad, which gave the sultans religious standing.

Cairo became the largest city of the Muslim world, full of mosques, schools and hospitals. The sultanate grew rich on the spice trade between the Indian Ocean and Venice. The Black Death hit it hard from 1347, and Portuguese ships later cut into the spice trade. The Ottomans conquered it in 1517.
